sources.summary: Original example: a=(3,4), b=(2,0). The dot product is 3×2 + 4×0 = 6.
Original example: (1,0) and (0,1) are nonzero perpendicular vectors, and their dot product is zero.
Original example: replacing (2,0) with (−2,0) flips the dot product with (3,4) from 6 to −6. A zero vector has zero dot product with every vector, but no defined angle.

slides.title: The geometry of a dot product
body: An original teaching example about coordinates, alignment and a boundary.
Synthetic sample, not a retrieved lecture.
slides.notes: All examples are original fixture content. Scene times are planned teaching segments, not a live retrieval.

slides.title: The coordinate calculation
slides.notes: Walk through the two products: 3×2 and 4×0.

slides.title: Direction changes the sign
body: Hold v = (3, 4) fixed. Reverse the second vector.
slides.notes: Only w changes sign, so both coordinate contributions change sign.

columns.title: w = (2, 0)
columns.body: The dot product is +6. The angle is acute.

columns.title: w = (−2, 0)
columns.body: The dot product is −6. The angle is obtuse.

slides.title: Zero can mean different things
body: The angle interpretation requires two nonzero vectors.
slides.notes: Zero is algebraically orthogonal to every vector, while its geometric angle is undefined.

slides.title: A prediction to test
body: Keep v = (3, 4). Double w from (1, 0) to (2, 0).
What happens to the dot product and the angle?
slides.notes: Generated extension: the dot product doubles from 3 to 6, while the angle stays approximately 53.13 degrees. Use the companion playground to verify.
slides.headline: Same direction. Twice the length.

slides.title: Coordinates and geometry agree
body: A dot product combines coordinate contributions into one number.
Its sign describes alignment when both vectors are nonzero.
slides.notes: The generated playground computes these exact relationships. It is not a measurement of learning outcomes.
slides.headline: Calculate, then interpret
